parts.text:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Your task now is to interview one future user and find out what they need. You will not see any other description of their work: what you learn, you learn from them.

What you know about the business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The users of the future service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You are now interviewing: a fleet technician. You will interview each of the other roles separately.

Cover at least these topics, in your own words and in whatever order the conversation allows:

- an ordinary working day, from start to end;
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad;
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it;
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong;
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong;
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them.

How to interview:

- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and open.
- Follow up wherever an answer is vague, general, or surprising. Ask for a concrete example.
- Do not suggest answers, features, or solutions, and do not describe how the service could work.
- Do not summarise the interview back to the interviewee.
- You can ask at most 30 questions in this interview.
- When every topic is covered and follow-ups no longer bring anything new, end by writing exactly `END OF INTERVIEW` on its own line, and nothing else in that message.

Write only your next question.
The interviewee is ready. Ask your first question.
Could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from start to finish?

I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order. Throughout the day, I add new drones to the fleet, retire old ones, and set up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back when they are fixed, and send drones to charge.
What is the very first thing you look at or do when your shift begins?
I don't know.
How do you find out which drones need repairs or charging during the day?
I don't know.
Who tells you when a drone needs attention, and who do you let know once it is ready again?
I don't know.
Could you tell me about the worst day you have had at work in the last few months, and what made it so bad?
I don't know.
Is there anything you check by hand today because you do not trust the current tools or information?
I don't know.
What are you most afraid a new software service would get wrong in your work?
I don't know.
When something goes wrong with a drone or a charging pad, what do you need to know right away?
I don't know.
Could you walk me through what happens when you add a new drone to the fleet?
I don't know.
What information do you record or look at when you set up a charging pad or send a drone to charge?
I don't know.
Are there times when you try to retire a drone, take it out of service, or send it to charge, and you cannot?
I don't know.
What differences are there among the drones or charging pads you work with?

We run several hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers. They differ in their carrying capacity, flight range on a full battery, carried sensors like cameras, thermal cameras, and laser scanners, and the charging connector types they use, which are not interchangeable. Each of our sites has its own charging pads, a few dozen in total.
How do the charging pads differ from one another, or across your sites?
Our drones use several charging connector types that are not interchangeable. We have a few dozen charging pads at our own sites. Pads are never lent to another company.
Can a charging pad break or go offline, and how do you handle it when that happens?
I don't know.
How does your work connect with the dispatchers or the airspace desk at your company?
I don't know.
What rules or restrictions apply when you take a drone out of service, retire it, or send it to charge?
I don't know.
What else do you keep track of about your sites, drones, or charging pads?

Each drone has a home site, and we run a few dozen charging pads at our sites. We keep our drones and charging equipment in working order, and repairs and servicing are carried out by us. Regulators can ask us to show how our drones have been looked after.
What exactly do regulators ask to see about how your drones have been looked after?
I don't know.
